title: Virtual environments & pip
summary: Create isolated Python environments and install packages with pip so each project keeps its own dependencies without conflicts.
objectives: Explain why each project needs its own isolated environment
Create a virtual environment with the venv module
Activate and deactivate an environment on Windows, macOS, and Linux
Install, upgrade, and remove packages with pip
Pin dependencies in a requirements.txt file and reinstall from it
Avoid committing your venv folder to Git with .gitignore

quiz.q: Why use a virtual environment for each project?
options: To isolate each project's packages and versions
quiz.why: A virtual environment keeps each project's dependencies separate, so different versions never clash.

quiz.q: Which command creates a new virtual environment in a folder called venv?
quiz.why: python -m venv venv runs the built-in venv module and creates the environment in a folder named venv.

options: Lists installed packages with exact versions
quiz.why: pip freeze prints every installed package and its exact version, which you redirect into requirements.txt.

quiz.q: Write the pip command that installs every package listed in requirements.txt.
quiz.why: The -r flag tells pip to read a requirements file and install each pinned package from it.

quiz.q: After activating a venv, what command leaves it and returns to the system Python?
quiz.why: Typing deactivate exits the active environment in any shell, restoring your normal Python.

quiz.q: True or false — you should commit your venv folder to Git so teammates get the same packages.
quiz.why: False. The venv is large and machine-specific; share requirements.txt instead and add venv to .gitignore.

body_markdown:
## The dependency problem

Real projects rely on **third-party packages** — code other people wrote, like `numpy` or `pandas`. The trouble is versions. Project A might need `pandas` version 1, while Project B needs version 2. If you install everything into one global Python, those versions fight, and upgrading for one project silently breaks another.

As a maths graduate think of it like keeping each experiment's variables separate so results don't contaminate each other.

## What a virtual environment is

A **virtual environment** (venv) is a private copy of Python with its own package folder, living inside your project. Packages you install there stay there. Python ships with a `venv` module, so you need nothing extra.

```bash
cd my_project
python -m venv venv
```

This creates a `venv` folder. It is *not* your code — never commit it to Git.

## Activating and deactivating

You must **activate** the environment so your terminal uses its Python. The command differs by operating system.

```bash
# Windows (PowerShell)
venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# macOS / Linux
source venv/bin/activate

# leave the environment
deactivate
```

Once active, your prompt shows `(venv)`. Now `python` and `pip` point inside the environment.

## Installing packages with pip

`pip` is Python's package installer. With the venv active, anything you install lands inside it.

```bash
pip install pandas
pip install numpy==1.26.4   # a specific version
pip list                    # see what's installed
pip uninstall pandas
```

## Sharing with requirements.txt

To let a teammate (or future you) recreate the exact setup, freeze your packages into a file and commit *that* file.

```bash
pip freeze > requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Add a `.gitignore` line containing `venv/` so the heavy environment folder is never committed.

## Your task

Create a fresh project folder, make a venv, activate it, install `requests`, and save a `requirements.txt`.

slides.title: Virtual environments & pip
slides.narration: Welcome back to Month One of your journey from maths graduate to A I engineer. In this lesson we tackle something every professional Python developer uses every single day: virtual environments and pip. By the end you'll be able to give each project its own isolated set of packages, install libraries cleanly, and share your exact setup with anyone.

slides.title: The dependency problem
bullets: Projects rely on third-party packages.
Different projects need different versions.
One global Python makes them clash.
Upgrading for one can break another.
slides.narration: Let's start with the problem. Real projects use packages other people wrote, like numpy or pandas. But here's the catch: one project might need version one of a package, while another needs version two. If you install everything into a single global Python, those versions fight each other, and fixing one project quietly breaks another.

slides.title: The solution: a venv
bullets: A virtual environment is a private Python.
Each project gets its own package folder.
Installs stay inside that project.
Built into Python — nothing to install.
slides.narration: The solution is a virtual environment, often shortened to venv. Think of it as a private copy of Python that lives inside your project, with its very own folder for packages. Anything you install there stays there and never touches other projects. Best of all, it's built right into Python, so there's nothing extra to download.

slides.title: Creating a venv
bullets: Move into your project folder first.
Run the venv module with python.
It creates a folder named venv.
slides.narration: Creating one is two short steps. First, move into your project folder. Then run python, dash m, venv, followed by a name for the folder, conventionally also called venv. That command builds a fresh, empty environment inside your project. Remember, this folder is not your code, so we'll never commit it to Git.

slides.title: Activating the venv
bullets: Activate so the shell uses its Python.
The command depends on your operating system.
Your prompt then shows (venv).
slides.code:
# Windows PowerShell
venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
# macOS / Linux
source venv/bin/activate
slides.narration: Creating the environment isn't enough; you have to activate it so your terminal actually uses its Python. The command differs by operating system. On Windows PowerShell you run the Activate dot p s one script inside venv, Scripts. On Mac or Linux you type source venv, bin, activate. Once it works, your prompt shows venv in brackets.

slides.title: Installing with pip
bullets: pip is Python's package installer.
Active venv means installs land inside it.
Pin an exact version with double equals.
pip list shows what you have.
slides.code:
pip install pandas
pip install numpy==1.26.4
pip list
slides.narration: Now for pip, Python's package installer. With your environment active, anything you install lands safely inside it. Type pip install, then the package name, to grab the latest version. If you need an exact version, add double equals and the version number. And pip list shows you everything currently installed in this environment.

slides.title: Removing and upgrading
bullets: Uninstall a package you no longer need.
Upgrade with the dash dash upgrade flag.
Keep environments lean and tidy.
slides.code:
pip uninstall pandas
pip install --upgrade requests
slides.narration: Managing packages goes both ways. When you no longer need something, pip uninstall removes it. To get a newer version of a package you already have, use pip install with the dash dash upgrade flag. Keeping your environment lean means fewer surprises and faster installs down the line.

slides.title: Sharing with requirements.txt
bullets: pip freeze lists exact versions.
Save it into requirements.txt.
Others reinstall with -r.
Commit the file, not the venv.
slides.code:
pip freeze > requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt
slides.narration: How do you give a teammate, or future you, the exact same setup? You freeze it. pip freeze prints every package with its exact version, and the greater-than sign saves that into a file called requirements dot t x t. Anyone can then recreate your environment with pip install, dash r, that file. You commit the file, never the venv folder.

slides.title: Ignore the venv in Git
bullets: The venv is large and machine-specific.
Add venv/ to your .gitignore.
Share requirements.txt instead.
slides.narration: One important habit: never commit your venv folder to Git. It's large, it's tied to your specific machine, and it can always be rebuilt. Instead, add a single line, venv slash, to your dot gitignore file. Then commit requirements dot t x t so others get the right packages without the bulky folder.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Forgetting to activate before installing.
Committing the venv folder to Git.
Wrong activate command for your OS.
Forgetting to update requirements.txt.
slides.narration: Let's flag the traps. One: installing packages before activating, so they land in the wrong place. Two: committing the heavy venv folder by accident. Three: using the wrong activate command for your operating system. And four: installing something new but forgetting to refresh requirements dot t x t. Watch for these and your projects will stay clean.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: A venv isolates each project's packages.
python -m venv venv, then activate.
pip installs; freeze pins versions.
Ignore venv; commit requirements.txt.
Task: make a venv and install requests.
slides.narration: Let's recap. A virtual environment gives every project its own isolated packages. You create one with python dash m venv, then activate it. pip installs and removes libraries, and pip freeze pins exact versions into requirements dot t x t. You ignore the venv folder in Git but commit the requirements file. Your task before the next lesson: create a fresh project, make a venv, activate it, install requests, and save a requirements file. Great work, and I'll see you in the next lesson.
